KMI-style Shariah screening on PSX

KMI and similar screens publish methodologies and stock lists so investors can see which companies currently meet a defined Shariah framework. Think of them as rulebooks with updates — not permanent halal stamps.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

Indexes vs personal rulings

An index methodology is one structured approach. Your advisor may add stricter filters or different interpretations.

Always know which list you are following and when it was last reviewed.

What typically gets examined

Public methodologies usually discuss business segments and selected financial ratios. The official documentation is the source of truth for definitions and thresholds.

Third-party apps and posts can lag behind reconstitutions — verify against the publisher when stakes are high.

Using a compliant universe in practice

Many investors build watchlists from a current universe, then apply normal fundamental analysis: profitability, debt, valuation and governance.

Screening answers “eligible under this method?” — not “will this make money?”

Portfolio hygiene still applies

If you invest in screened names, track lots, dividends and sells like any other portfolio. Faith-conscious investing does not remove the need for records or risk management.

This guide is educational only. It is not investment, tax, legal or religious advice. Rules, fees and tax rates change — confirm details with your broker, SECP/PSX sources, FBR guidance and qualified advisors before you act.

What gets published

A KMI-style screen publishes two things you should insist on seeing together: the methodology, and the list of constituents produced by that methodology on a date. The methodology says which businesses are excluded and which financial ratios are tested, against which totals, with which cutoffs. The list is the output. Either piece alone is an advertisement.

The publisher can revise the method. A cutoff you memorized may be the previous notice. Read the notice that matches the list you are using, and keep the PDF. A blog summary is not the notice.

Indexes also have weight rules, caps, and rebalance dates. Those affect the index level. They are a separate document from the question of whether a given company passed the screen.

How to read a constituent list

Find the company, the symbol, and the effective date. Check whether the list you have is the index, a watchlist for possible inclusion, or a list of deletions. People circulate screenshots that mix those categories.

A company on the list has passed the published tests for that period. It has not been declared suitable for you. Your financing, your broker arrangement, and the scholar you follow can still put the share outside your own rule. A company off the list has failed the published tests or was not eligible. It is not automatically forbidden by every method in the world. It failed this one.

Additions and deletions are the useful part of the announcement. A deletion is a prompt to re-read the accounts, not an instruction from this website to sell. A purchase or a sale is your decision, made with the notice in front of you.

Ratios without the statements are rumors

If you want to understand a borderline name, open the annual or quarterly accounts and identify the lines the methodology names. Debt, interest income, and non-compliant income are defined in the method. They are not “whatever a forum called debt.” Write the figure, the page, and the period.

Interim accounts can move a ratio across a cutoff before the next index review. The index will not update on the morning the accounts are filed. If your rule is “I follow the index,” wait for the index. If your rule is “I apply the method myself,” do the arithmetic and accept that you may disagree with the index until it rebalances.

Do not let a portfolio app’s sector label stand in for this work. Sector labels group businesses for browsing. They are not the screen.

Funds that say they follow a screen

An Islamic equity fund’s offering document should say which screen it uses and what it does when a holding falls outside the screen. Read that policy. The fund’s name is not the policy. The factsheet’s top holdings are a snapshot, not the policy either.

You still own units of the fund, not a personal copy of the index. The manager’s tracking difference, cash, and fees mean your units are not identical to the index level. Judge the fund by its document and its reports.

A conventional equity fund can hold many of the same companies without applying the screen. Do not infer a screen from a familiar ticker in the top-ten list.

Keep the decision dated

When you buy or decide not to, note the list date and the document you relied on. Six months later the list may have changed and you will want to know what you knew then. The tracker’s notes and the trade date are a reasonable place. The ruling, if you sought one, lives with you, not in the app.

Re-read on a schedule you can keep, perhaps when each new list is published, rather than every red day. A price move is not a change in the company’s debt ratio. Save the PDF of the list next to the trade note so the date and the methodology version stay attached to the decision.

PSX Tracker will not stamp a ticker as compliant. Use the publisher methodology and, where you need it, a qualified scholar. This guide only tells you how to hold those documents up to the light. If a later list removes a holding, the trade date in your ledger shows that you bought it while it was still on the earlier list.

Common questions

What is a KMI-style screen?

A published set of business and financial tests used to build a Shariah equity list. The list and the rules can change.

If a stock is on the list, is it halal for me?

Not automatically. Use the published methodology and personal scholarly guidance rather than a ticker’s presence alone.

Where should I read the rules?

From the index publisher’s own methodology, not from a summary in a portfolio app.
